Chapter 3: Understanding How to Work and Learn Most Effectively
When it comes to getting the most out of your work and learning, it’s not just about knowing your strengths—it’s about really understanding *how* you work best. We all have our unique ways of tackling tasks, processing information, and connecting with others. Recognizing what makes you tick is the secret to building a personal approach that’s both productive and genuinely satisfying.
One of the biggest differences you'll notice among people? It’s whether they’re readers or listeners. Maybe you’re someone who soaks up information through reading. Or perhaps you need to hear ideas out loud for them to really stick. This simple distinction can have a huge impact on how you perform. Imagine a manager who’s a strong reader—they might find meetings challenging if most of the information is shared verbally. On the flip side, a listener might feel bogged down by endless written reports.
So, how do you figure out your learning style? Well, start by thinking back—when did information really sink in for you? Was it when you read it, or when you heard someone explain it? You can also try mixing things up. Experiment with different formats and notice which one helps you understand and remember more.
Your environment matters, too. Some people absolutely thrive with clear routines and a set structure. Others? They do their best work when they have more flexibility and can go with the flow. Maybe you get a buzz from working with a team, bouncing ideas around. Or, perhaps you feel most focused when you’re working solo, with no distractions. Figuring out what energizes you can help you make better choices—whether it’s about the roles you take, the projects you choose, or even how you set up your daily schedule.
Here are some questions you might ask yourself: Do you get more done in a quiet space, or do you need the hum of a busy environment? Does a set routine make you feel secure, or does it feel like it’s holding you back? And when it comes to hitting your goals, do you find it easier working on your own, or as part of a group?
There’s also the way you make decisions. Some people are comfortable deciding quickly, even if they don’t have all the details. Others need to collect information and take time to reflect before making a move. There’s no right or wrong here—what matters is finding what works for you, and leads you to the best results.
Once you’ve got a sense of your preferences, the next step is to shape your work and learning environment around them. Maybe that means asking for written summaries if verbal instructions are hard to follow. Or, seeking out roles that give you the right balance of structure and freedom. Sometimes, it’s about building routines that match your natural rhythms of focus and energy.
It’s also worth remembering—other people probably have different styles from yours. If you want to work well together, you’ve got to appreciate those differences and be willing to adapt. Think about a colleague who loves detailed written plans—if you’re more of a ‘talk it out’ person, you’ll both need to meet each other halfway. By recognizing and respecting these different approaches, you’ll build stronger, more productive relationships.
And here’s something important—your own preferences aren’t set in stone. As your roles shift and new challenges pop up, what works for you might change. So, keep reflecting, keep experimenting, and stay open to tweaking your approach. That way, you’ll keep finding new ways to work and learn that truly fit you.
